'''Carel S. Scholten''' (Amsterdam, 1925 – 2009) was a [[physicist]] and a pioneer of [[computing]].

He went to the [[Vossius Gymnasium]] in Amsterdam and then studied [[physics]] from 1945 to 1952 at the [[University of Amsterdam]].

In 1947 he was asked by the Dutch ''Mathematisch Centrum'' (which later became the [[Centrum Wiskunde & Informatica]]) to collaborate in building an automatic calculator with his friend and fellow student [[Bram Loopstra]]. Their first system, the [[ARRA (computer)|ARRA I]] was not a success, but its successor, the [[ARRA II (computer)|ARRA II]], on which [[Gerrit Blaauw]] also collaborated, was.

In 1954 work started on the [[ARMAC (computer)|ARMAC]], which he built together with Loopstra and [[Edsger W. Dijkstra]], who was responsible for the software and collaborated with Scholten for more than 30 years.
The ARMAC was remarkable for its use of [[transistor]]s.

In 1958 Scholten went to work for [[Electrologica]] (later [[Philips]] Electrologica), where he developed the [[Electrologica X1]] computer with Loopstra; up to 1964, 40 models were installed, mainly at universities. He remained with Philips Electrologica until 1979, when he switched to the [[Philips Natuurkundig Laboratorium]], where he stayed until 1985.

In 1991 he was awarded an [[honorary doctorate]] by [[Technische Universiteit Eindhoven]].

== Publications ==
* [[Edsger W. Dijkstra]] and Carel S. Scholten (1990). ''Predicate Calculus and Program Semantics''. Springer-Verlag {{ISBN|0-387-96957-8}} – An abstract, formal treatment of [[Predicate transformer semantics]]<ref>{{cite web|title=Edsger Wybe Dijkstra|url=http://www-groups.dcs.st-and.ac.uk/~history/Biographies/Dijkstra.html|work=School of Mathematical and Computational Sciences|publisher=University of St Andrews|accessdate=26 December 2010}}</ref>
